content: A counterfeit drug, also known as a counterfeit medicine, is a pharmaceutical product that is manufactured and distributed with the intent to mislead consumers about its origin, authenticity, or effectiveness. These drugs are often referred to colloquially as beat bags or bunk bags. Counterfeit drugs may lack active ingredients, contain insufficient amounts of active ingredients, or include entirely incorrect active ingredients, which may or may not be harmful. They are typically sold in packaging that is inaccurate, misleading, or entirely fake. Counterfeit medicines and generic drugs that are intentionally mislabeled to deceive consumers are classified as counterfeit. However, a drug that has not received regulatory approval is not necessarily counterfeit. Counterfeit drugs can be categorized based on specific characteristics, such as: Drugs that have been relabeled after their expiration, deemed defective, or otherwise unfit for use. Drugs in which the active ingredient has been fraudulently diluted and then relabeled. Drugs in which the active ingredient has been adulterated and then relabeled. Drugs in which the active ingredient has been substituted with another substance and then relabeled. Substances falsely labeled to misrepresent the active ingredient entirely. Substances falsely labeled where the combined active ingredients meet one or more of the above criteria. The use of counterfeit medications can lead to serious health consequences, including unexpected side effects, allergic reactions, or worsening of the patient’s medical condition. Many counterfeit drugs contain no active ingredients at all, instead consisting of inert substances that provide no therapeutic benefit. Others may contain incorrect ingredients, improper dosages of the correct ingredients, or even hazardous substances. The true extent of the counterfeit drug problem is unknown due to the difficulty in detecting, investigating, and quantifying such cases. However, it is known that counterfeit drugs are a global issue, with a higher prevalence in developing countries. Estimates suggest that up to 10% of drugs worldwide are counterfeit, and in some countries, more than 50% of the drug supply consists of counterfeit products. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that the annual revenue generated by counterfeit drugs exceeds $32 billion. Several technologies have been developed to combat counterfeit drugs. For example, radio frequency identification (RFID) uses electronic devices to track and identify pharmaceutical products by assigning unique serial numbers to their containers. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is working on an electronic pedigree (ePedigree) system to track drugs from manufacturing facilities to pharmacies. This system aims to prevent drug diversion and counterfeiting by enabling wholesalers and pharmacists to verify the identity and dosage of individual products. Additionally, techniques such as Raman spectroscopy and Energy Dispersive X-Ray Diffraction (EDXRD) can detect counterfeit drugs without opening their packaging. Many counterfeit drugs sold in developing countries or online originate from China. The Chinese State Food and Drug Administration does not regulate pharmaceutical ingredients manufactured and exported by chemical companies. This regulatory gap has been widely criticized internationally, but a lack of cooperation from Chinese regulatory agencies has hindered effective oversight. In response to the growing problem, the WHO established the Rapid Alert System (RAS) on May 6, 2005, the first web-based system for tracking counterfeit drug activities. India has also been identified as a major source of counterfeit drugs. According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), 75% of counterfeit drugs globally originate from India, followed by 7% from Egypt and 6% from China. While it is illegal to produce counterfeit drugs for domestic use in India, it is not against the law to manufacture counterfeit drugs for export. Counterfeit antibiotics with low concentrations of active ingredients pose a significant global threat. Incomplete courses of antibiotics allow bacteria to survive and develop resistance, exacerbating the problem of antimicrobial resistance. The issue of counterfeit drugs has also been highlighted in media reports. For example, the BBC and other outlets have reported on Dr. Dora Akunyili, a Nigerian woman appointed to address the problem of counterfeit drugs. These reports indicate that many counterfeit drugs originate from the same countries that produce legitimate pharmaceuticals, particularly China and India.
